newsitem.title: USA: White House unruffled by reported budget defection.
newsitem.headline: White House unruffled by reported budget defection.

text.p: House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt will vote against President Bill Clinton's budget deal with the Republicans, a Democratic aide said on Tuesday, but the White House shrugged off Gephardt's defection.

"We've got a lot of Democrats and a lot of Republicans in support of the budget agreement, and we understand and respect those with divergent views," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said as reports spread through the U.S. capital that Gephardt was deserting Clinton on the budget issue.

Gephardt, a potential rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000, planned to tell fellow Democrats of his decision at a meeting on Tuesday, a Democratic aide said.

"At the (Democratic) caucus, he is going to say he is going to vote against it and why," the aide said. He noted that the decision was consistent with Gephardt's statements around the country in the past two years that he would not vote to cut Medicare to fund tax cuts that benefit the wealthy.
Echoing the White House line, Gore said, "If he does do that, then the only thing I would say in response is I respect his views."

Asked if he believed the Missouri Democrat was positioning himself to challenge for the presidency three years from now, Gore replied: "Oh, I have no idea about anything like that. These are important issues that are deserving of full discussion and debate, and I respect differing opinions."

The agreement would balance the budget by cutting spending by $304 billion over the next five years below what would have been spent without changes in policy. Much of the difference comes from almost $130 billion in savings in Medicare and Medicaid.
The deal also provides for a net $85 billion tax cut by 2002 and gives Clinton $33 billion for domestic goals.
Gephardt has "strong feelings on that (agreement), and we respect his strong feelings," McCurry said.

Asked if Clinton's congressional lieutenant had told the White House of his intention to oppose the budget agreement, McCurry said, "I think we've got a pretty good sense of what he's thinking and feeling."

Gephardt's defection inevitably evoked memories of Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich's 1990 stand on a budget agreement between then President George Bush and the Democrats, who controlled Congress.
Although Gingrich was not speaker at the time, he was able to torpedo the deal and sorely embarrass Bush by forging a strange-bedfellow coalition of conservative Republicans and liberal Democrats.
McCurry said he saw no resemblance between then and now.
"Two entirely different situations. Two entirely different moments in history. I don't see any comparison," he said.
